html:
Directory of Ecumenism

Importance of this Directory

1The mystery of the Church dwells in the mystery of wisdom and goodness of God whom draws to all human family and even the entire creation towards the perfect unity, towards Him.

2The religious reality of the world presents to the Catholic Church and next to her, a constellation of churches and creeds separated from her through the century; and so forth there is also the other part constituted for those who do not accept Christ and those who do not know or believe in God yet. To all of them, the Church directs her maternal solicitude and her responsibility before God.

3Two parts of the humanity are not Christians yet; 52% are Catholics; 18% orthodox and 30% are Protestants. The redemptive mission that is directed to those non Christians (the gentiles) is known as “mission ad gentes”; the work inside the Catholic Church with the children of God is called “apostolic work”; finally, the mission addressed to non Catholics Christians is known with the name of Ecumenism.

4Nowadays, our Institute faces entirely with this problem of no Christianity in the world. Therefore, our firm decision is to go there, whenever we may be called, it means to say, to all the world (Mk 16,15), never avoiding the missionary adventure that makes us to see the reality of our religion and the increase of lack of faith. Our apostolic work in places of a very old protestant tradition, schismatic-orthodox, or the reality of the increasing of mixes matrimonies in many countries; our commitment for the evangelization of the culture, which includes universities, schools, etc. places where we will find men and women of different ideas or beliefs. All this things demand from us a good preparation, a good formation, to be religious of clear convictions not only in terms of preparation for the mission ad gentes but also in respect with those who are not Catholics. To serve the Church is to serve the unity. To serve the Church is to serve Christ in his purpose of gathered all the children of God who are separated in one only flock (Jn:11,52), and to renovate everything in Him, submitting all this to the Father so that we may be an eternal praise in the Spirit. This is a big task! A task that is worthy of all our energies. A task that can overwhelmed our own strength. A task that demands from us continual prayer.

5For this reason, the Holy Father emphasize: “I think that the work for the unity of Christians is one the greatest and most beautiful works of the Catholic Church in our times”. He also adds, “The ecumenical dialogue is the fundamental task of the Church of the year 2000.”

In all this reasons we find the real importance for our Directory in Ecumenism.

II

Catholic Notion on Ecumenism

Chapter 1. Catholic Church and Church of Christ

6We just have said in the first part that the mystery of the Church is inside of the divine plan of salvation for all men. To this end, God sent into the world His only Son, who was raised up on the cross, entered into glory and poured out the Holy Spirit through whom he calls and draws into unity of faith, hope and charity the people of the New Covenant which is the Church. In order to establish this holy Church in every place until the end of the ages, Christ entrusted to the college of the Twelve to which he chose Peter as head, the office of teaching, ruling and sanctifying. It is the will of Jesus Christ, that through the faithful preaching of the Gospel, the administration of the sacraments, and through government in love exercised by the apostles and their successors under the action of the Holy Spirit, this people should grow and its communion be made ever more perfect.

7The Church founded by Jesus Christ, says the Council, subsists in the Catholic Church. It means, that the Church is that community of believers, or faithful founded by Jesus Christ on Peter and confirmed on the day of Pentecost. On this way, the Catholic Church believes and professes that she is the only Church of Jesus Christ without deficiency in any substantial element given (granted) by his founder.

8For this: Catholics hold the firm conviction that the one Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church "which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the Bishops in communion with him".22 They confess that the entirety of revealed truth, of sacraments, and of ministry that Christ gave for the building up of his Church and the carrying out of its mission is found within the Catholic communion of the Church. Certainly Catholics know that personally they have not made full use of and do not make full use of the means of grace with which the Church is endowed. For all that, Catholics never lose confidence in the Church. Their faith assures them that it remains "the worthy bride of the Lord, ceaselessly renewing herself through the action of the Holy Spirit until, through the cross, she may attain to that light which knows no setting".23 Therefore, when Catholics use the words "Churches", "other Churches", "other Churches and ecclesial Communities" etc., to refer to those who are not in full communion with the Catholic Church, this firm conviction and confession of faith must always be kept in mind.

9Extra ecclesia nulla salus: It is a firm and strong conviction in the Catholic Faith that “is through Catholic Church alone, which is the all embracing means of salvations, that the fullness of the means of salvation can be attained. It was to the apostolic college alone, of which Peter is the head, that we believe our Lord entrusted all the blessings of the New Covenant, in order to establish on earth the one Body of Christ into which all those should be fully incorporated who already belong in any way to God’s People. This is the doctrine of the traditional principle Extra ecclesia nulla salus; outside of the Church there is no salvation; only in Her we can find the fullness for all ways of salvation and it is through Her and in order to Her that the Holy Spirit incites the hearts of those who are not united in a perfect way to the sanctifying grace.

10The Catechism of the Catholic Church explains the sense in which this principle should be understood:

"How are we to understand this affirmation, often repeated by the Church Fathers?[Cf. Cyprian, Ep. 73.21: PL 3, 1169; De unit.: PL 4, 509-536.] Re-formulated positively, it means that all salvation comes from Christ the Head through the Church which is his Body:

Basing itself on Scripture and Tradition, the Council teaches that the Church, a pilgrim now on earth, is necessary for salvation: the one Christ is the mediator and the way of salvation; he is present to us in his body which is the Church. He himself explicitly asserted the necessity of faith and Baptism, and thereby affirmed at the same time the necessity of the Church which men enter through Baptism as through a door. Hence they could not be saved who, knowing that the Catholic Church was founded as necessary by God through Christ, would refuse either to enter it or to remain in it.[LG 14; cf. Mk 16:16 ; Jn 3:5 .] "

"This affirmation is not aimed at those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ and his Church:

Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who nevertheless seek God with a sincere heart, and, moved by grace, try in their actions to do his will as they know it through the dictates of their conscience - those too may achieve eternal salvation.[LG 16; cf. DS 3866-3872.] "

"'Although in ways known to himself God can lead those who, through no fault of their own, are ignorant of the Gospel, to that faith without which it is impossible to please him, the Church still has the obligation and also the sacred right to evangelize all men.'[AG 7; cf. Heb 11:6 ; 1 Cor 9:16 .]"

Chapter 2: The unity of the Church according to the will of Christ

11The Church is a kind of sacrament of intimate union with God, and of the unity of all mankind. She is the People of God, that through the action of the Holy Spirit and the mystery of the death and resurrection of Christ, gathers all men and women of every nation and culture in order to build up the body of Christ. And so we shall all come together to that oneness in our faith and in our knowledge of the Son of God; we shall become mature people, reaching to the very height of Christ’s full stature. (Eph.4:12-13). Therefore, the unity of the People of God is an essential constitutive of the Church. This unity performs the koinonia/ or communion though faith, the sacramental life and the hierarchical minister. For this reason one of the essential characteristics of the Church is the Unity.

12The Holy Father expressed that: “the unity, is the summit of Christ’s prayer in the Last Supper, it is His testament of love, the commandment He has left to us before His passion “so that the world will believe that you sent me”. If we are not one, like the Father is one in Christ, and Christ is one with the Father, the world will not believe;

13“The unity of the Church indisputable belongs to her essence. She is not the end in herself. The Lord gives her to us so that the world may believe. (Jn.17:21).

14The communion in which Christians believe and for which they hope is, in its deepest reality, their unity with the Father through Christ in the Spirit. Since Pentecost, it has been given and received in the Church, the communion of saints. It is accomplished fully in the glory of heaven, but is already realized in the Church on earth as it journeys towards that fullness. Those who live united in faith, hope and love, in mutual service, in common teaching and sacraments, under the guidance of their pastors 18 are part of that communion which constitutes the Church of God. This communion is realized concretely in the particular Churches, each of which is gathered together around its Bishop. In each of these "the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church of Christ is truly present and alive".19 This communion is, by its very nature, universal.

15Unity, is the expressed will of Christ (that all be one) and it is also Christ’s will that this unity can be a sing of credibility for the world (May they be one, so that the world will believe that you sent me). Then, the will of Christ, the testimony that we should give of Christ, is the principal reason that should move us to work without resting in this task.

16Without doubt, we understand that all discord openly contradicts the will of Christ, provides a stumbling block to the world, and inflicts damage on the most holy cause of proclaiming the good news to every creature, because when those who invoke Christ are divided among themselves, it is like if Christ would be divided: “Is Christ divided? (1Cor1:13).

17John Paul II has insistently repeated that the drama of the division of Christians is a cause of scandal:

- It is incredible that in this days we have to live the drama of division among Christians, which is cause of perplexity and scandal.

- All kind of divisions are not tolerable among Christians.

- Without unity Christians are incapable of giving a satisfactory testimony of Christ, and their division is still an scandal for the whole world, most especially in the young churches born in the lands of mission.

- The unity is a characteristic and an exigency of the Catholic Church. All divisions and divergences are contrary to the plan of God.

Chapter 3: Ecumenism as Grace

18Having in mind that the unity of Christians is the will of Christ, and that the search for this unity is the end of ecumenism, it is evident that authentic and true ecumenism is not a purely human project, nor is it explained adequately by the most noble aspirations of men of good will. On the contrary, ecumenism supposes a divine grace, a supernatural motion, that moves the children of God to traverse the difficult way toward the reconstruction of unity. “The ecumenical movement tries to be a response to the gift of the grace of God, that calls all Christians to faith in the mystery of the Church, following the design of God that wishes to lead humanity to salvation and to unity in Christ by the Holy Spirit.” 1

19“But remember that the unity that Christ wants for His Church is His proper gift.”2 “The unity, definitively, is a gift from God, a gift for which we should ask and prepare ourselves that He may grant it to us. Unity, the same as any gift, as every grace, depends ‘on God who has mercy’ (Romans 9:16). Because the reconciliation of all Christians ‘surpasses human strength and capacity,’ 3 continual and fervent prayer manifests our hope, that does not deceive, and our trust in the Lord that He will make all things new (Romans 5:5, Rev. 21:5)”4

20“Unity can only be granted to us as a gift by the Lord as a fruit of His passion and of His resurrection in the opportune ‘fullness of times.”’5

21The ecumenical labor demands a special charity, patience, hard work to get rid of all discouragement, absolute fidelity to the truth, delicacy, and tact, docility to the inspirations of the Holy Spirit and a constant asceticism. This can only be fruit of the love of the cross and of the gifts of the Holy Spirit: “The ecumenical movement is a grace of God, given by the Father in response to the prayer of Jesus6 and the supplications of the Church inspired by the Holy Spirit.7”8.

Chapter 4: To whom ecumenism is directed

22“The plenitude of the unity of the Church of Christ has been maintained in the Catholic Church, while other churches and ecclesial communities, while not being in full communion with the Catholic Church, conserve in reality a certain communion with her”9.

23The ecumenical work revolves around those non-Catholic Christians that keep a singular relation of belonging in respect to the Catholic Church.

24In all truth, all men can call themselves in some way members of the Church. We can distinguish different degrees of belonging:

251) Full Members: Those who have a full incorporation in the Catholic Church “They are found in full communion with the Catholic Church, on this earth, the baptized who unite themselves to Christ within Her visible structure. It is to say by the means of the profession of faith, of the Sacraments, and of the ecclesiastic regime.”10 This is judged through two elements that determine the belonging to the Church. One is the apostolic faith (dogmatic and sacramental; that which also includes the hierarchical union with the successors of the apostles, it is their responsibility to watch and guarantee the faith: instituyo doce para que estuvieran con el y para mandarlos a predicar11 and also go to all the world and preach the Gospel…he who believes…will be saved12 and among these to Peter and his successor: Simon, Yo he rogado por ti para que to fe no desfallezca, y tu, cuando te conviertas confirma a tus hermanos13.) The second element consists in the supernatural life that is produced by the Holy Spirit, living in the hearts of His faithful. These two elements properly constitute the man of the New Law, that which already is consists in ‘the grace of the Holy Spirit who is given to us by the faith of Christ”14. Among these members we must distinguish those who possess the two elements and those who are lacking the second.:

26a) The just: “To the society of the Church are fully incorporated, those who having the Spirit of Christ, accept entirely Her organization and all the means of salvation deposited in Her, and through the bonds of the profession of the faith, of the Sacraments, of the ecclesiastical system and of the communion, are united in Her visible body with Christ, who guides her by means of the Supreme Pontiff and the Bishops”15. Pius XII wrote: “Among the members of the Church should only be counted those who have received the washing of regeneration, and professed the true faith, and have not been separated from the unity of the Body, nor have been separated by the legitimate authority for grave acts admitidos.”16

27b) The Catholic sinners who have not defected from the faith: “Nevertheless, will not reach salvation, even though they are incorporated in the Church, he who does not persevere in charity, remains in the womb of the Church with the ‘body’, but not with the heart.”17

282) Not full members: Those who lack the fullness of the apostolic faith, whether it be because they do not entirely possess its dogmatic and sacramental aspect, or because they do not have unity of regime, that is to say, the hierarchical communion with Peter who is the guardian of the faith: “The Church feels united by various bonds with all those who honor the name of Christian, by being baptized, even though they do not entirely profess the faith, or do not conserve the unity of communion under the successor of Peter. Many conserve Sacred Scripture as a norm of faith and of life, and manifest religious zeal, believe in the love of God the Father all powerful, and in Christ the Son of God and Savior, are marked with baptism by which they are united to Christ, and recognize and accept in their own churches and ecclesial communities other Sacraments. Many of them also have the episcopate, celebrate the Holy Eucharist and encourage piety toward the Virgin Mother of God. To these is added also the communion of prayers and of other spiritual benefits; even more, a certain true union in the Holy Spirit, through who also works in them with His sanctifying virtue by means of gifts and graces, and some of them until He gives them the strength of martyrdom. This is how the Spirit promotes in all the disciples of Christ the desire and the actuation so that all unite peacefully in one flock and under only one Shepherd, as Christ had determined. To obtain this, Mother Church should never stop praying, hoping, and working, and to all her children exhort them to sanctify and renew themselves in such a way that the image of Christ shines more clearly over the face of the Church.”18.

29Evidently, the degree of more or less imperfection depends on the plenitude of the professed faith and the conception about the Primacy of Peter in each concrete Church. The situations are not equal with the Christians who are only schismatic and those with whom the Church has serious and profound dogmatic questions. For this reason the Pope John Paul II speaks of the oriental Christians as with whom we have “an almost full communion, even though it is still imperfect”19.

30Leaving clearly the doctrine about the absolute identity of the Church founded by Jesus Christ with the Catholic Church, it can be accepted the expression that signifies in the rest of the churches and Christian ecclesial communities the existence of vestigia Ecclesiae, vestiges of the Church; taken in a good sense, this means that the Catholic Church recognizes in other separated churches elements of truth and of life that she Herself possesses in plenitude20.

313) Members in potency. “Those who have not yet received the Gospel, in diverse forms they are ordained to the People of God. In the first place, the people to whom the covenants and the promises, and of whom Christ was born according to the flesh, according to the election, most beloved of His parents, because the gifts and the vocation of God are irrevocable. The plan of salvation also embraces those who recognize the Creator, and among them in first place, the Moslems, who, making the profession of faith of Abraham, adore with us only one God, merciful, who will judge men in the last day. This same God is neither far from others who among shadows and images look for the unknown God, through whom he gives life to all, the inspiration of all things, and as Savior wants all men to be saved. In fact, those who inculpably do not know the Gospel of Christ and His Church, but go searching with sincerity for God and under the influence of grace try to comply with the works of His will, known by the judgment of the conscience, can reach eternal salvation”21. They, “by a certain unconscious desire and aspiration are ordained to the Mystical Body of the Redeemer”22.

32The ecumenical work is aimed towards those whom we have designated as not full members, while the potential members are object of the mission ad gentes.

33Therefore, ecumenism begins from and is founded in a certain imperfect communion of faith in the “Triune God and...Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior”23.

Chapter 5: The end of Ecumenism: Unity

34Ecumenism begins from an undeniable act: “ no Christian can feel themselves satisfied with these imperfect forms of communion. They do not correspond to the will of Christ, and debilitate His Church in the exercise of His mission”24.

35The ultimate end of the ecumenical movement is to reach full visible communion of all Christians: “…Have as specific mission the reestablishment of the unity among Christians”25.

36Ecumenism is the search for unity. However, it must be kept in mind that when the Catholic Church aspires to unity it is not supposed that unity does not already exist. It does exist in Her as unity of faith, of worship (sacramental) and of government. It is more, it is the unity that Christ gave when He founded Her, and that has not stopped existing throughout the historical vicissitudes through which She has passed. This is the way The Council’s expression “subsist in Her” can be understood.26 This unity, which is an essential and distinctive note, is supported visibly, by the expressed will of Christ, held up by the Apostle Peter and His successors.

37This unity is unity of the faith: “The decree (Unitatis Redintegratio) defines this unity as consistent ‘in the profession of only one fatih27. John Paul II said at the beginning of His Pontificate that the end of ecumenism is “to conquer the obstacles that separate us from the unanimous profession of the same faith”28. And later: “The integrity of the apostolic faith, as much as has been transmitted to us by the saints forever in the Apostolic Tradition (cf. Judas 3), must be conserved fully if we want our unity to be the unity for which Christ prayed…As in the times of St. Paul, also now all our strength to reestablish the unity between Christians would be in vain if it is not realized with total fidelity to the faith in Christ transmitted by the Apostles”29.

38It is unity in worship and in the sacraments: “…in the common celebration of Divine worship”30. John Paul II expressed this saying: “This suffering should stimulate us to conquer the obstacles that still separate us from the profession of the same faith, and the reunification of our separated communities with a same sacramental ministry”31.

39It is unity in concord: “…in the fraternal concord of the family of God”32.

40It is the unity in an external bond, that can not be anything other than Peter: “…this unity, that demands, by its own nature, a full visible communion of all Christians, it is the ultimate end of the ecumenical movement”33. To express this in some way, John Paul II says: “By sending St. Augustine to preach the Gospel to the Anglo Saxon people, St. Gregory fulfilled the pastoral and missionary responsibility proper of the ministry of the Bishop of Rome. In his writings we discover a rich and profound appreciation of the universal primacy given to the bishop who occupies the Seat of Peter. It was he who called the Bishop of Rome ‘caput fidei’ and who described him as he who performs this ministry as ‘servus servorum Dei’34... Today the divisions among Christians demand that the primacy of the Bishop of Rome will be also a primacy in the action and initiative in favor of unity that Christ prayed for so fervently”35

41This will of Christ to found upon Peter, has its base revealed in the text of Mt. 16, 18-19: I tell you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of the netherworld will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of Heaven and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in Heaven and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in Heaven.. The ecumenical unity can never disregard this fundamental text and its right interpretation.

42Peter is the source of the unity: “So that the episcopate itself was one and indivisible, He established the blessed Peter ahead of the rest of the Apostles, and instituted in him the principle and fundament, perpetual and visible, of the unity of faith and communion”36

43“Unity” signifies “unity under Peter in the Catholic Church”, in which Christ, as the Council says, “...chose Peter and gave him all the sheep so that he would confirm them in the faith and that they would graze in a perfect unity.”37

Chapter 6: Ecumenical Cause of the Ecumenical Unity: The Holy Spirit

44The Church in Her ecumenical hope looks, not at the human strength, but at the power of God: “this holy desire of reconciliation of all Christians in the unity of one unique Church of Jesus Christ goes beyond the human strength and capacity. She places all her hope in the prayer of Christ for the Church, in the love of the Father towards us, in the power of the Holy Spirit. Y la esperanza no quedara fallida, pues el amor de Dios se ha difundido en nuestros corazones por medio del Espiritu Santo, que nos ha sido dado (Rom 5:5)38

45“The Holy Spirit that lives in the believers, and fills, and governs all the Church, actualizes this admirable communion and unites all so intimately in Christ, who is the Beginning of the unity of the Church”39. The ecumenical unity “deals with the same unity that Christ prayed for and that the Holy Spirit actualizes”40. For this reason, the unity that is fruit of Ecumenism is asked by the Church in a deprecativa form:

46Pius XI: “And our blessing, hecha plegaria, reaches the throne of God and repeats to Him the supplication that, precisely in these days, the Divine Spirit put on the lips and in the heart of His Church: that He deign to call all those who have gone astray to the unity of the Church..., we pray, hear us”41

47Pius XII: “We wish and want that all who carry en the heart the anxious call to embrace Christian unity-and nobody who is of Christ values little such a great thing-make petitions and prayers to God, who is author of order, unity, beauty, so that the praiseworthy wishes of all the good are not slow to be brought to effect”42.

48Vatican Council II: “I beg insistently to all Christians, as much the eastern as the western, to present to God fervent, and continual, daily prayers, so that with the help of the Most Holy Mother of God, all will become only one thing.”43.

49John XXIII: “That they may be one! This is the sketch of the divine Redeemer that we should realize, venerable brothers, and it is a grave work confided to the conscience of every one…This beat of the Heart of Christ should invite us to a renewed proposal of surrender so that among the Catholics belong the love and the testimony toward the first mark of the Church (one) and so that en the vast horizon of the Christian denominations, and beyond, that unity will be realized, towards that which rises the aspiration of the right and generous hearts”44

50Pablo VI: “If only the most benign Redeemer, who, being at the point of death, prayed to the Father so that all those who would believe in Him were only one, as He and the Father are one (Jn. 17: 20-21), He would deign to hear this most ardent desire of ours and of the Universal Church, that we all celebrate with only one voice and only one faith the mystery of the Eucharist and made participants of the body of Christ, we make ourselves only one Body, compaginado by the same ligaduras with which He wished to constitute it! (1 Cor. 10:17)”45.

51If the peace of the world and the restoration of all the things in Christ can only be the work of God (St. Pius X call it Opus Dei46), with equal or more reason the work of the unity of the Church would also be the work of God, to which Pius XI calls opus in primis Dei: “This realization of the union will not be done by human appearance but rather by the goodness of God, who is not an aceptador of persons (Act 10:34)…But already that reunion of all the people in the ecumenical unity, as principle work of God, can be reached with the divine help and assistance, we insist in pious prayers, following the examples and teachings of St. Josafat, that worked for the unity above all with the pwer of prayer”47.

52To none of the quoted Pontiffs escapes the miraculous dimension of this unity. It is more, it is precisely its miraculous nature that gives the character of sign of credibility that brings to the recognition of Jesus Christ: That all may be one, as You, Father, in me and I in You, that also they may be one in us, so that the world believes that you sent me48. For example:

53Leo XIII, in his prayer for the conversion of the Hebrews and the Turkss (1899): “Oh sweet Heart of Mary!, tell Jesus for we neither know nor can tell Him, and He will listen to you…and to overcome the resistance of those for whom we pray, a miracle is necessary, of Immaculate Virgin! We ask you through the immense love that you have for Jesus. Ah, yes, deign to appear to the Hebrew and Turks, as you appeared to Ratisbon, and at a sign of your right hand, they, as he, will convert! Oh come, come soon the day in which the most Holy Trinity reigns through You in all hearts and that all may know, love, and adore in spirit and truth the divine fruit of your womb, Jesus!”49.

54Paul VI asked in the Grottaferrata abbey: “the complete Catholic unity, so that it can flourish under our eyes, in our history full of suffering, the evidence of a miracle in which we are one flock under only one shepherd”50.

55Paul VI: “As you know, this problem of the ‘union of the Christians in the unity of the Church’ is of great importance and actuality, and we should confront it, even though it may encounter many difficulties. Divine help is more necessary than ever, as a miracle of the Lord. But perhaps the hour is near. Here it is necessary to pray much”51.

56For this reason John Paul II, indicated that, in the example of the Virgin Mary, the “docility to the Holy Spirit…is the most profound center of the ecumenical attitude”52

Chapter 7: Formal Cause of the Ecumenical Unity

57The formal cause of all society consists in a certain order, which is to say, in the particular relation that is established among its members in order to a common end; this way, the formal principle is that which is able to establish the knots of union and mutual ordering among its members.

58We can say that the formal cause of the ecumenical unity is in some way attributed to grace53, because among the Christians all the relations, inasmuch as the Christians, suppose and proceed from the created grace. It is grace that establishes the fundamental incorporation into God, as the same is participation of the Divine Nature54. The grace of the Christian comes from the plenitude of the grace of Christ; as St. Thomas says: “The principle of the new law is constituted by the grace of the Holy Spirit, who is manifested in the living faith by charity. Now then, men obtain this grace through the Son of God made man, by whose humanity was first filled by grace (replevit gratia), to derive itself later in us. For this reason it says in Jn. 1:14: The Word was made flesh; and later it adds: full of grace and truth, and further (v. 16): Of His fullness we have all received, grace upon grace. To which is added (v. 17) that the grace and truth have come through Jesus Christ”55.

59The grace of the Christian is derived from the grace of the Son, and we are made sons by adoption; consencuentemente hermana a los hombres entre sí. From the grace come the rest of the bonds of union:

-From her comes the faith that unites the faithful in the profession of the same revealed truth

-From her comes the hope that unites the travelers in the same supernatural hope.

-From her comes the charity that unites in a most excellent way (“Proprium amoris est unire”56) the faithful with God and among themselves; for this reason St. Paul calls it the “Bond of perfection”57.

60It is also the grace that truly unites the Christians amongst themselves; and as the Holy Spirit is He who does the work of grace, He establishes mysterious bonds that escape the visible dimensions of the Church: they are these that invisibly belong to the visible Church.

Chapter 8: Ecumenical Hope

61It is evident that the Church directs enconados efforts to procure unity; it would fit then to ask through the hope that she will reach what she looks for: In what is it founded, what certainty does it possess, which is its precise object?

Article 1: The fundament

62The fundament of the ecumenical hope of the Church supports itself basically in

a prophecy and in a prayer of Christ Himself.

63a) The prophecy. St. John 10:16 reminds us: Tengo otras ovejas que no son de este redil, y es preciso que Yo las traiga, y orian mi voz, y habra un solo rebano y un solo pastor. The prophetic character of the verse shows itself by its own wording, which is put in the future –will hear, will be-and the affirmation of the unconditional future in the mouth of God is prophecy in a strict sense. This is the way it is understood by the Holy Fathers, Pontiffs, and Councils who have used this text in a prophetic sense58. St. John Chrysostom affirms: “does not indicate necessity but rather a future thing with certainty”59, and St. Jerome: “that which even though in part we see actualized in the Church every day, however, more fully will be realized in the consummation of the world and in the second coming of the Savior”60. To support the prophetic character of this passage is also used the Pauline prophecy which can be considered as the parallel: “..........” (Rms. 11: 25-26)

64b) Prayer. The prayer is that which Jesus makes in the Last Supper, before His passion: That they may all be one, as You, Father in me and I in You, that also they may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me (Jn. 17:21) This unity asked by Jesus had been identified by numerous Fathers, Doctors, Pontiffs, with the ecumenical unity. Dealing with an absolute prayer of Christ, its efficacy is certain and infallible.

Article 2: The certainty

65The certainty comes from the character of these two texts: from the prophetic character of one, and from the character of the efficacious prayer of the second.

Article 3: The object of the hope of the Church

66The object of the hope of this hope, is to say, what it is that is concretely hoped for, is contained in the exegesis and use that the Tradition and the Magisterium have made of these biblical texts; in a summarized form:

67-The sheep fold to which have been incorporated “the other sheep” that Christ has, has been identified with the Catholic Church and with the communion with the Apostolic See of Rome.

68–The other sheep are all those who are outside of the Catholic Church founded by Christ upon Peter and the Apostles, in whatever time and place. In the text of St. Paul, he speaks of plentitude; it should be understood as a moral plenitude, not mathematical, which is to say, that which men habitually understand as “the entire world”, without this excluding the existence of non-Catholic minority groups, or non Christians61.

69–The shepherd in some texts is Christ62, in others is Peter and the Roman Pontiff, successor of Peter and Vicar of Christ63. In general terms, the habitual usage of the Johannie text that Tradition has made, Christ can not be separated from Peter and his successors.

70Therefore, the object of ecumenical hope of the Church is the future (but historical, before the Second coming of the Savior) union of the plenitude of men and of the churches under the one flock shepherded by Peter, Vicar of Christ.

Part III

The Exercise of Ecumenism

71For a fruitful exercise of ecumenism, the Church has elaborated a series of norms that should guide all ecumenical activity.

Chapter 1: Necessity of Institutional Renovation

The true ecumenism should begin with the presentation of the Catholic Church Itself. The Church will lose credibility if it proposes a restoration of the unity of Christians and at the same time will present lack of unity and holiness in itself. “Christ calls to the pilgrim Church on its journey, to this everlasting reform, of that which the Church itself, as a human institution, always has necessity...This reform has an extraordinary ecumenical importance”64.

72In this way we can point out the great enemies of ecumenism from the point of view of the example of the Church:

-Lack of unity. The lack of unity among the Catholic faithful is an enemy of ecumenism: the faults against the submission to the authentic hierarchy, the faults against the common patrimony of the faith (work of theological contestary), the faults against the unity, fruit of the fostering of false dialectics (Church of the poor and Church of the rich; high theology and low theology; white theology and black theology, etc). The faults against the Catholic liturgy, freeing Her to improvisation, to chaos, to contradiction. In this sense, progressivism, the Marxist theology of liberation, the contestary moral theology, etc., are enemies of the authentic ecumenism. We will work in favor of ecumenism in the measure that we sew unity of faith, of government, of worship.

73–Lack of holiness. Holiness is a mark of the true Church founded by Christ in which the union that ecumenism looks for should be actualized; therefore, it is a sin against ecumenism to present an image of the Church stripped of Her holiness. In this sense, all sin, but particularly the sin of scandal (principally the sin of Her shepherds), destroys the ecumenical work. Work in favor of ecumenism is when the works of mercy are lived in plenitude. Charity towards the poor, the sick, the most in need; the example of those who live radically the evangelical counsels; the example of the martyrs; this is that which moves to ecumenical unity.

74–Lack of catholicity: it is to say lack of spirit and missionary impetus. Loss of the missionary fervor is sin against ecumenism, the lack of conviction in the evangelical mandate of Jesus Christ, because precisely this is that which manifests to the Church founded by Him.

75–Lack of apostolicity: it is to say lack of love of Peter and his successors, the contempt of his teachings, of his directives, the desgano or lack of concern for the following of his initiatives, his particular intentions, his missionary plans. When this occurs, it is not in the beating of the heart of the Church.

76For this the exercise of ecumenism imposes a renewal and revitalization:

1) Institutional: giving examples of poverty, undertaking works of charity, of beneficence, asistenciales, of service, founding missionary works, etc.

2) Liturgy: to present the captivating richness of Catholic worship, respecting the diversity of the rites (latin, ukrainian, coptic, malabar, etc.) Realizing our liturgy with solemnity and sacredness; showing the centrality of worship in the life and spirituality of the Church.

3)Doctrinal: presenting the faith with profundity and clarity; reevaluating the biblical, theological, patristic, and philosophical studies. Not hiding the truth but rather showing its splendor. It is important to emphasize that one of the arguments often by the converts to Catholicism has been and is the seeing of the Catholic Church as a body of solid, sure, and guaranteed doctrine.

Chapter 2: The demand of personal renewal

“Even though the Catholic Church possesses all the revealed truth of God, and all the instruments of grace, however, her members do not live with all the fervor they should. Therefore the face of the Church shines less before the eyes of our separated brethren and of all the world, and for this the growth of the kingdom of God is slowed. All Catholics should tend to Christian perfection and, each one according to his condition, work so that the Church, carrier-in Her body- of humility and of mortification of Jesus Christ, each day will be purified and renewed more, until She is presented to Christ glorious, and without stain or wrinkle”65.

John Paul II said: “Unity can only be fruit of a conversion to Christ, who is the Head of the Body who is the Church. This conversion should be profound and embrace the entirety of the members in the multiple aspects of their life, in such a way that the unity is truly realized”66.

“True ecumenism does not exist without interior conversion. In effect, the desires of unity come from and mature in the renewal of the soul, in the abnegation of self and in the generous effusion of charity. For this we have implored from the Holy Spirit the grace of sincere abnegation, of the humility and of the meekness in our service and of the fraternal generosity of the soul towards others…Remember all the faithful who will better realize and promote the union of the Christians, how much more they try to live a purer life, that is conformed to the Gospel. Because as tight is their communion with the Father, with the Word and with the Spirit, so much more intimate and easily will they be able to increase the mutual fraternity”67.

John Paul II said: “You can not have unity among brothers, if they do not have profound union-of life, of thought, of soul, of proposals, of imitation-with Christ Jesus; more over, if an intimate search of interior life in the union with the Trinity Itself does not exist …”68

Chapter 3: Principality of the “Spiritual ecumenism” or primacy of prayer

81We have said that the principle author of Ecumenism is the Holy Spirit, that the ecumenical unity is a grace, that the return to the unity surpasses human strength. From there the primacy in the work for unity is given to prayer. The ecumenical fruits do not come principally from meetings and dialogues, but rather fundamentally from the prayer to God.

82“All of us recognize the great value of prayer to realize that which is humanly difficult and perhaps impossible. Jesus Himself has told us: ‘that which is impossible to men, is possible for God’ (Lk. 18:27). We know what is important is to go to God humbly, day after day, asking Him the gift of continual conversion of life, that is so narrowly bound with the question of the unity of the Christians”69.

83“This conversion of heart and this holiness of life, together with the private and public prayers for the unity of the Christians, have been considered as the soul of all the ecumenical movement, and can rightly be called spiritual ecumenism”70.

Chapter 4: Necessity of a Specific Ecumenical Formation

84An important point upon which the Magisterium insists is the necessity, growing more and more, of the general ecumenical formation of the faithful and in particular of the priests. John Paul II said: “With a growing urgency, in the theological formation, and above all in that of the future priests, is required an ecumenical dimension, really founded and always assured. The Second Vatican Council has clearly pointed out this necessity71 : “...also the Catholics consecrated to the missionary works in the same regions where other Christians work, it is convenient today in a special way that they know the problems and the fruits that come from the Ecumenism in their apostolate”72. The actual demands of the mission of the Church makes precise an ecumenical collaboration that can not be put into practice without an appropriate spiritual, doctrinal, and cultural preparation”73.

85“Ecumenical Formation” means the preparation to confront this work of promoting the ecumenical unity. It begins by being conscience of the position that Ecumenism has inside the Church and of its mission, of the responsibility that the Church has before Jesus Christ to search for this unity, of the urgency of the work for unity in our age. It demands the knowledge of the history of the Church, of the divisions, of the doctrinal differences; it requires the knowledge of the peculiarities of the other Churches and ecclesiastical communities separated from the Catholic Church. It demands, also a solid formation in the Faith, an ecclesiological security, to be able to give reason before the other confessions of “the motives of our hope”74 .

86This formation should happen in the faithful in general, through the listening and studying of the Word of God, the preaching (in particular about the mystery of the unity of the Church), catechesis, liturgy (especially with prayer for the unity of Christians), spiritual life ( reminding the faithful of the importance of personal conversion to aspire to unity)75.

87In as much as the ordinary ministers, it is convenient to present to them the ecumenical dimension of the distinct subjects that they study throughout their formation76, offering to them if it is possible a special course about Ecumenism77.

88It is to desire also that some aspire (lay faithful or priests) to specialize in the ecumenical disciplines78.

Chapter 5: Respect for the legitimate diversity in the unity

89Diversity and unity are not contradictory, because the diversity can reduce itself to unity by harmony. Accidental diversity of liturgical, spiritual, and even disciplinary elements inside the Church, harmonized among themselves, contribute to manifest externally the immense richness of the Catholic Church: “Guarding the unity in the necessary, all in the Church, each one according to the function given to him, guard the due liberty, in the diverse forms of the spiritual life and of the discipline as in the variety of the liturgical rites; and even in the theological evolution of the revealed truth; but in all practice charity. And this way they will manifest each day more fully the true Catholicity and Apostolicity of the Church”79.

Chapter 6: Demands of a just valuation

90“On the other hand, it is necessary that the Catholics recognize and appreciate with joy the truly Christian values proceeding from common patrimony, that are found in our separated brethren. It is just and healthy to recognize the richness of Christ and the virtuous works in the life of all those who give testimony to Christ, sometimes, with the pouring out of their blood; because God is always admirable and worthy to be admired in His works. Neither should be forgotten that all that the grace of the Holy Spirit works in the hearts of the separated brethren can contribute also to our edification. That which is truly Christian can never be opposed to the authentic values of the faith; before the contrary, all can contribute to what is reached most perfectly the mystery of Chris and of the Church”80.

Chapter 7: Climate of Authentic Dialogue and Search for unity in the Truth

91Dialogue is fundamental to reestablish the discrepancies produced as an effect of the division and to dissipate those who have been cause of the disunion. St. Peter warns us that we should be always ready to give reason for our hope: dispuesto siempre para la defensa de la esperanza que abrigais, respondiendo a todo el que os pida razon acerca de ella (1 Pt. 3:15) Jesus Christ Himself gave us example of His magisterial pedagogy speaking with the Samaritan woman81, with His disciples82, with His enemies to lead them to the truth83.

92Paul VI has pointed out as characteristics of the dialogue:

a) Clarity above all: The dialogue supposes and demands intelligibility; it is an interchange of thought; it demands our apostolic diligence to make our language understandable.

93b) Meekness: That to which Jesus Christ Himself exhorts us (Learn from Me to be meek and humble of heart [Mt. 11:29]). “The dialogue is not prideful, nor is iriente, nor is it offensive. Its authority is instrinsic through the truth that it exposes, through the charity that it spreads, through the example that it proposes; it is not a commandment nor an imposition. It is peaceful, avoiding the violent methods, it is patient, it is generous84.

94c) Confidence: As much in the value of the word itself as in the disposition of the speakers to receive it.

95d) The pedagogical prudence: that has very much in mind the psychological and moral conditions of those who hear.

96e) Integrity: The presentation of the truth must be authentic and integral. “The solicitude to approach the brothers should not translate in a extenuation or in a diminishing of the truth. Our dialogue can not be a weakness in front of the duties of our faith. The apostolate can not compromise with a type of ambiguous engagement in respect to the principles of thought and action that must be a sign of our Christian profession. Irony and syncretism are forms of skepticism in respect to the strength and content of the word of God that we want to preach. Only he who is faithful enough to the doctrine of Christ can be effectively an apostle. And only he who lives with plenitude the Christian vocation can be immune to the contagion of the errors with those who he in contact”85.

97The ecumenical dialogue, and especially the theological dialogue should not be superficial because it deals with delicate and profound questions: “If for almost one millennium, the Oriental and Occidental (western) Churches have not celebrated the Eucharist together, this means that they have argued over grave problems”86.

98The unity that Ecumenism looks for can not only not disregard the truth, but rather it is the unity in the truth itself. As John Paul II has vigorously and beautifully said: “We should not resign ourselves to what the disciples of Christ do not give before the world the testimony of unity. This requires an unbreakable faithfulness to the truth, an attentive opening to the rest, a sober patience on the way and a love full of delicacy. Compromises do not work; it is only worth that unity that the Lord Himself has founded: the unity in truth and in love. It is heard now being said many times over that the ecumenical movement among the churches are at a standstill, that after spring appearing of the Council has come an age of frailty. Despite some difficulties that are to me lamented, I can not be in agreement with this judgment. The unity that comes from God He has given us from the cross. We are not permitted to want avoid the cross for the end of obtaining a rapid harmonization of the differences, putting between parentheses the question of truth. However, we are not permitting to renounce ones to another, to disregard ones to another, because the patient and sacrificed love of the Crucified demands from us that we get near to one another. We do not let ourselves part from the fatigue on the way, which will be to choose aparentes atajos that are nothing but deviations”87.

Part IV

False Conceptions about Ecumenism

Chapter 1: Errors by defect

100All vision of Ecumenism is false that sees in this phenomenon a novelty that arises in the Church from the Second Vatican Council. Ecumenism, as we have already established, belongs to the mission of the Church Itself, as Jesus Christ had established it. To consider it as a “novelty” is fruit of a defective ecclesiology, of a ignorance of the Tradition and History of the Church, and of a bad understanding of the will of Our Lord explicit in the Sermon of the Last Supper, as it appears in the Gospel of St. John88.

101Many are obstinate to the efforts realized and are indifferent to this particular mission of the Church. Of them John Paul II said at the beginning of his Pontificate: “There are persons who, finding themselves in front of the difficulties or also judging negatively the results of the initial ecumenical works, they would rather have preferred to throw themselves behind. Some express the opinion that these efforts are damaging to the cause of the Gospel, lead to a further rupture of the Church, provoke confusion of ideas in the questions of faith and morals, abocan a specific indifferentism...To all those that for whatever motive wish to dissuade the Church from the search for universal unity of Christians, they must be told one more time: Is it licit for us not to do it?”89.

Chapter 2: Errors by excess: Ecumenism as Religious Syncretism

102All the practices and conceptions that are seen in this movement a tendency to form a Super Church also destroy the true Ecumenism. They are fruit of the manocomunación of all the present Churches, including there the Catholic Church as one more. This is an ecumenism that is anti-christian, anti-catholic, and anti-evangelic. A similar conception of Ecumenism is a threat against the identity of the Church.

103In practice, this is proposed in two levels:

a) Those who aspire to a purely pragmatic unity, in which each one will conserve his proper belief to the personal title. They are those who think that Ecumenism consists in reuniting to march together, while what each one thinks is not that important90.

b) Those who aspire to a dogmatic unity, establishing for this Super Church a super dogma that disposes the elements that create “difficulty” to the union; particularly the Catholic doctrine about the Primacy of Peter, the Pontifical infallibility, the Sacramental doctrine (in a special way the Eucharistic doctrine and the ministerial priesthood), etc.

104It would fit to remember one more time the words of the Holy Father John Paul II: “The true ecumenical activity means opening, closeness, good disposition to dialogue, common search for the truth in the full evangelical and Christian meaning; but in no way does it mean nor can it mean to renounce or cause prejudice of some way to the treasures of divine truth, constantly confessed and taught by the Church...This does not mean absolutely losing the certainty of the proper faith, or weaken the moral principles, through whose lack will be felt very soon in the life of whole societies, determining among other things deplorable consequences”91.

105This in no way can help the cause of unity of Christians. What is more, we should say that the best way to desvirtuar the ecumenical ideal is to contaminate it with ambiguous generosities, with calculated silences, with false tolerances (especially in the sacramental area)92; all this proceeds more from the weakness or from the astuteness of the men than from the clear, strong, faithfulness of the adopted children of God.

106True Ecumenism is destroyed when the Catholic theologians work neglecting the principles of Catholic theology; when they work with the principle of sola Scriptura, neglecting the Tradition, the Magisterium, and the everlasting philosophy. Also when specific aspects of the faith or of the structure of the Catholic Church are presented dark or veiled, particularly the sacramental doctrine about the ministerial priesthood, the Eucharist, the forgiveness of sins through individual confession, the indissolubility of matrimony. This cannot contribute to unity; while, on the contrary, the clear definitions of the proper faith serve all, including the speaker; it should never be forgotten that the dialogue can make deeper and purify the Catholic faith, but can change it. It can be applied here that which John Paul II said: “The reason of a certain number of difficulties to believe and of individual and collective religious crises, is in that which relitivizes the absolute and absolutizes the relative”93.
